title: Viscosity and Newtonian fluids: a fluid's internal friction
examples: Why does ketchup flow when you shake it?

explain.say: Pour water and honey side by side. The honey crawls. That stickiness, the internal friction of a fluid, is viscosity. Your car engine relies on it: a thin oil film keeps metal parts apart. Look at the board: oil trapped between a moving plate and a fixed one.

explain.say: The oil touching each plate sticks to it. This is the no-slip condition. So the oil layers slide over each other, fastest at the top, still at the bottom. The rate the speed changes across the gap is the shear rate: 2 metres per second over 1 millimetre, that is 2000 per second. See the layers?

explain.say: Newton's law of viscosity says shear stress equals mu, the dynamic viscosity, times the shear rate. Engine oil has mu about 0.1 pascal seconds; water only 0.001. So the stress on the plate is 0.1 times 2000, which is 200 pascals. Which needs more force to drag, an oil film or a water film?

explain.say: Oil, a hundred times more! Now the graph. For a Newtonian fluid, like water, air or oil, stress is a straight line through zero: viscosity stays constant. Paint and ketchup are shear-thinning: they flow more easily the faster you shear them. Cornflour in water is shear-thickening: it stiffens.

Brilliant. That is why paint spreads easily under the brush yet does not drip off the wall. Real link: heating a liquid lowers its viscosity, but heating a gas raises it. Challenge: why must engine oil have a viscosity grade for winter?

draw.text: Liquids thin when hot; gases get more viscous

faq.a: A real fluid touching a solid surface moves with that surface, so its speed at a fixed wall is zero. The layers further out slide over it.
A fluid whose shear stress is directly proportional to shear rate, so its viscosity does not change with how fast it is sheared. Water, air and most oils are Newtonian.
A fluid whose apparent viscosity falls as it is sheared faster. Paint, ketchup and blood are shear-thinning.
asks: why does ketchup flow when you shake it

faq.a: A fluid that gets stiffer when sheared fast, like a thick mix of cornflour and water. You can run across it but sink if you stand still.
Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flowing, its internal friction. Dynamic viscosity mu is shear stress divided by shear rate, in pascal seconds.

facts: The viscosity of water at 20 °C is about 0.001 Pa·s.
Liquids become less viscous when heated, while gases become more viscous.

quiz.say: Water with a viscosity of 0.001 pascal seconds fills a 0.5 millimetre gap under a plate moving at 1 metre per second. What is the shear stress?
quiz.show: Water (μ = 0.001 Pa·s), gap 0.5 mm, plate speed 1 m/s. Shear stress?

wrong.1: That treats the gap as 2 mm or forgets to convert millimetres to metres properly.
wrong.2: That is the shear rate, not the stress; multiply by the viscosity.

quiz.say: On a graph of shear stress against shear rate, what does a Newtonian fluid look like?
quiz.show: Shear stress vs shear rate: a Newtonian fluid is…

options.show: A straight line through the origin
options.say: A straight line through the origin

quiz.why: Constant viscosity means stress is proportional to shear rate: a straight line through zero.

wrong.1: A flattening curve is shear-thinning, like paint.
wrong.2: A steepening curve is shear-thickening, like cornflour and water.
